personality_voice.book_baseline: Across all seven books, Ron's personality is defined by a consistent and recognizable cluster: loyal, brave, and genuinely warm, but also insecure, reactive, prone to jealousy, and capable of petty cruelty toward those he loves. His voice is colloquial, direct, and emotionally unguarded — short sentences, rhetorical questions, blunt assessments, self-deprecating humor, and occasional unexpected tenderness. He deflects anxiety with jokes, expresses jealousy clumsily, and shows moral clarity in moments of crisis. Crucially, he is not simply comic relief: he is a co-investigator, a strategist, and an emotional anchor who is also capable of sustained unpleasantness. His personality across the series is defined as much by his flaws — weeks of cold-shouldering Hermione in HBP and GoF, petty cruelty about girls at the Yule Ball, the departure in DH, sustained aggression during the GoF estrangement — as by his virtues. The insecurity of being the sixth Weasley son, perpetually in Harry's shadow, is the foundational psychological texture confirmed structurally by the Mirror of Erised in PS.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Ron's core personality markers consistently across all eight entries: his humor is present throughout (the spider butterflies line in CoS, 'kill us faster' in PS, 'Wankers' in HBP, 'That's unfortunate' in DH); his loyalty is unwavering and well-performed; his bluntness survives in multiple exchanges ('She's a nightmare, honestly'; 'Piss off' to Percy; 'Not bloody likely'); his bravery in crisis is preserved (chess chamber, Shrieking Shack, Department of Mysteries, Horcrux destructions). The love-potion sequence in HBP, the Deluminator speech in DH, and the spider-fear sequences in CoS and PoA all represent the films at their most characterologically faithful to Ron's voice.
personality_voice.difference: The films systematically remove the sustained unpleasantness that is one of Ron's defining characteristics in the books. The weeks-long cold-shouldering of Hermione in HBP, the extended GoF estrangement, the sustained pettiness in OotP's Quidditch Keeper arc — all compressed into single scenes or removed entirely. The foundational insecurity about being the sixth Weasley son, the texture that the Mirror of Erised confirms, is largely absent from the theatrical films (the Mirror scene is cut from PS theatrical release). His wit is sharper and more inventive in the books; the film Ron is funnier in broad strokes but less verbally precise. Across the series, the film consistently prioritizes Ron's warmth and humor at the expense of his capacity for petty cruelty, prolonged dysfunction, and the specific social anxiety of perpetual secondness. Books 5 and 6 represent the worst failures: in OotP virtually every subplot that gives Ron complexity (Quidditch Keeper arc, prefect badge, Percy's letter) is absent; in HBP the weeks of emotional deterioration are replaced by episodic comedy. The most important books for Ron's series-wide arc — GoF (jealousy/estrangement), OotP (insecurity/triumph), HBP (romantic arc), and DH (maturation/co-protagonist status) — all show meaningful personality compression.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The per-book scores ranged from 17 (GoF, OotP) to 20 (PoA), with most clustering at 17–18. The two most important books for Ron's series-wide personality — OotP and HBP, where his flaws and complexity are most fully dramatized — both scored 17, reflecting significant simplification. PoA's 20 is the high-water mark because that film happened to preserve his voice most densely. The synthesis score of 17 reflects: core personality consistently present and well-performed; secondary layer of sustained unpleasantness, insecurity texture, and wit systematically stripped; no major trait inverted but the defining psychological architecture (the sixth-son insecurity) largely absent from theatrical films. The 17 sits at the lower end of the 'main personality preserved, notable simplification of secondary traits' band, weighted toward GoF and OotP losses.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Across the series, Ron is an active co-protagonist whose narrative agency is substantial and varied. He is the character who knows the wizarding world and explains it to Harry (and the reader). He is the chess sacrifice in PS, the Polyjuice co-architect in CoS, the Scabbers/Pettigrew link in PoA, the investigative co-theorist across GoF, the Quidditch Keeper arc center in OotP, the Horcrux-planning leader in DH, the Chamber-of-Secrets-entry originator in DH. He initiates plans (ghoul plan, Norbert-to-Charlie, Ministry infiltration), provides intelligence others lack (Unbreakable Vow consequences in HBP, Magical Maintenance uniforms, Potterwatch), and performs decisive actions at key turning points (Expelliarmus alongside Hermione against Snape in PoA, Imperio on Bogrod in DH, Parseltongue entry into Chamber in DH). His absence during estrangement in GoF is itself narratively significant — Harry is genuinely weakened without him.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve Ron's most dramatically visible acts of agency: the chess sacrifice (PS), the forest drive and rockfall guard (CoS), the Shrieking Shack sacrifice (PoA), the Yule Ball scenes (GoF), the Umbridge distraction (OotP), the Horcrux destructions and Chamber entry (DH). His role as Harry's companion and emotional validator is consistently maintained. The Polyjuice participation (CoS), the Imperio casting (DH), and the Parseltongue entry (DH) are all preserved and represent the films' most faithful renderings of his agency.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The films systematically strip Ron's intellectual and investigative agency, transferring much of it to Hermione. The Flamel discovery (PS), the Riddle award deduction (CoS), the Buckbeak defense research (PoA), the cave-scene analysis and Bagman/leprechaun-gold theorizing (GoF), the Potterwatch discovery and sustained leadership during Harry's Hallows obsession (DH), and the ghoul plan (DH) are all absent or reduced. The Joint Expelliarmus against Snape (PoA) is cut, Harry acting alone. Ron's entire Quidditch Keeper arc (OotP), which is the book's primary narrative spine for his character, is largely absent from the theatrical film. The climactic DA defense of Hogwarts (HBP) is cut. His role as theorist, planner, and intelligence-gatherer is the single most consistently lost dimension across all seven films. What remains is primarily his role as emotional validator and brave combatant — important functions, but a substantial reduction from the books.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 13 (PS, CoS, HBP, GoF, OotP, DH) to 14 (PoA, DH). The narrow range reflects a consistent pattern: his dramatic agency is preserved, his intellectual and investigative agency is systematically transferred or removed. The synthesis score of 13 reflects: dramatic role intact and well-performed in most films; intellectual co-protagonist function substantially diminished across the entire series; multiple specific acts of initiative transferred to Hermione (the Transfer Rule penalizes this consistently); OotP's near-total absence of his Quidditch arc and DH's absence of the ghoul plan and Potterwatch as the worst individual failures. Weighted toward the most agency-critical books (GoF, OotP, DH), 13 is the appropriate synthesis.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ron's motivations are layered throughout the series but have a consistent core: love for Harry and Hermione as chosen family; terror of being inadequate — as a friend, a Keeper, a son, a wizard; the deep insecurity of being the sixth Weasley, always in Harry's shadow; family loyalty coexisting with family shame about poverty. His internal conflicts are specific: jealousy of Krum (GoF, OotP) that is really displaced romantic feeling for Hermione; the estrangement from Harry in GoF driven by years of accumulated secondness; the departure in DH where real insecurities are amplified by the Horcrux. His motivations are almost always correct in the books but rarely stated — they are dramatized through sustained behavior across chapters.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the correct motivational direction consistently. Loyalty to Harry and Hermione, family love, insecurity about adequacy — all are present in every film in some form. The departure scene in DH explicitly names his jealousy and family fear. The Deluminator speech names his redemptive guilt. The GoF confrontation scene ('Ron Weasley, Harry Potter's stupid friend') articulates his shadow-anxiety more directly than any single book passage. The family fear motivation is present in every appearance of the Weasley family.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films state motivations more bluntly and less through accumulated evidence. In the books, Ron's motivations are built across weeks of observable behavior — the sustained estrangement in GoF, the weeks of Quidditch dysfunction in HBP and OotP, the Potterwatch obsession in DH — that make the motivations feel lived-in rather than declared. The film versions tend to compress motivation to a single confrontation scene per book that explicitly names the conflict, losing the texture of motivation expressed behaviorally over time. The insecurity about being the sixth Weasley son — confirmed by the Mirror of Erised, built across dozens of small moments in PS — is substantially absent from theatrical films. His complicated family-loyalty conflict (Percy in OotP, the ghoul plan logic in DH) is largely absent. The internal conflict about adequacy in the Quidditch Keeper arc (OotP) is unfilmed.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 10 (OotP) to 12 (PoA, DH), with most at 11. OotP's 10 reflects the most severe simplification — the Quidditch Keeper arc's entire motivational architecture is absent. The synthesis score of 11 reflects: core motivational direction consistently correct; specific texture of insecurity-as-behavior largely absent; motivations stated rather than dramatized; the most important motivational vehicle (the sixth-son insecurity across the full series) substantially underexplained in theatrical films. Weighted toward OotP and GoF as the books where motivation is most richly dramatized and most compressed in film.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ron has both a book-level arc in each volume and a series-level arc across all seven. The series arc is a maturation from insecure, reactive boy into a co-equal hero who chooses his loyalties deliberately. Key arc stages: PS (recognition by Dumbledore, first individual triumph); CoS (tested loyalty, courage under pressure); PoA (sacrifice, moral clarity about betrayal); GoF (estrangement and reconciliation, incomplete emotional growth); OotP (failure and triumph as Quidditch Keeper, first independent recognition via prefect badge); HBP (romantic arc with Hermione, commitment to the Horcrux hunt); DH (departure, return, maturation, co-protagonist status in the final battle). The series arc is explicitly resolved when Ron stands at Voldemort's defiance and fights alongside Harry and Hermione as an equal, having chosen them over safety.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films preserve the arc's major endpoints and most emotionally visible pivot points: the chess sacrifice recognition (PS), the Shrieking Shack sacrifice (PoA), the GoF reconciliation, the HBP hospital scene and commitment to accompany Harry, the DH departure and return, the Horcrux destructions, the Chamber of Secrets initiative, and the final battle. The series ends with Ron in the right place emotionally and narratively. Rupert Grint's performance consistently conveys warmth, growth, and deepening commitment across the eight films.
character_arc.difference: Almost every individual book arc is missing important developmental steps. PS's arc lacks its starting-point texture (sixth-son insecurity). GoF's arc compresses the weeks of estrangement into one scene, making the reconciliation feel less earned. OotP's primary arc (Quidditch Keeper arc) is entirely absent — the film Ron has no arc in OotP, entering and exiting in the same condition. HBP's arc is present in emotional peaks but missing the sustained low points that give the recovery its weight. DH's arc is missing the middle section where Ron proves himself through sustained daily leadership rather than single dramatic acts. The series-level arc's connective tissue — the slow accumulation of Ron growing from boy to man across seven years of tested loyalty — is significantly thinned because so many of the intermediate steps in individual books are absent. What survives is a series of emotional high points without the sustained groundwork.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
character_arc.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 9 (HBP, OotP) to 11 (PS, PoA, DH), with CoS and GoF at 10. OotP's 9 is the worst failure — no discernible arc in the theatrical film. HBP's 9 reflects the missing low points. The synthesis score of 10 reflects: series arc's major endpoints and dramatic pivot points preserved; individual book arcs consistently missing important developmental steps; the series-level maturation arc readable but significantly thinned; OotP and HBP as the worst individual failures weighted appropriately. The 10 sits at the upper boundary of the 'incomplete, missing important steps' band — recognizable arc, destination correct, but too many rungs of the ladder removed to score higher.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ron has three defining relationships across the series: (1) Harry — equal co-protagonist friendship defined by mutual loyalty, complementary skills, and the specific dynamic of Ron knowing the wizarding world while Harry knows the non-magical one; the relationship includes estrangements (GoF, DH), genuine tension (OotP when Harry considers withholding Order information), and ultimately co-equal standing; (2) Hermione — the most emotionally complex and sustained relationship arc in the series, moving from hostility through bickering partnership to romantic love, expressed through jealousy, protectiveness, banter, and tenderness; (3) his family — particularly the weight of being one of seven, the Weasley family warmth, the poverty-and-pride tension, and specific family dynamics (Percy's betrayal in OotP, the ghoul plan logic of protecting his family in DH, Fred's death). Secondary: Sirius (GoF), Hagrid (consistent warmth across all books), Ginny (protective dynamic).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Ron friendship is the most faithfully preserved relationship across all films — the warmth, the ease, the mutual backing, and the estrangement-and-reconciliation beats are consistently rendered. The Hermione-Ron relationship is present in every film in its jealousy and banter dimensions and reaches its emotional peaks (hospital scene in HBP, Deluminator speech in DH, reunion in DH). The Weasley family warmth is consistently present. The most important Hermione-Ron emotional beats (hospital scene, the kiss implied in the Horcrux destruction, the final commitment) survive.
key_relationships.difference: The Hermione-Ron relationship loses its nurturing-warmth dimension in almost every film — the handkerchief scene in DH, the multiple book-moments of Ron comforting Hermione, the sustained quiet protectiveness — are largely absent, leaving the relationship skewed toward jealousy and banter. The relationship's full emotional complexity is therefore underrepresented. The Harry-Ron relationship loses its 'Ron as anchor when Harry is passive' dynamic (most significant in DH) and the daily-texture of co-equal partnership across OotP and GoF. The family relationships are most significantly diminished in OotP (Percy's betrayal arc entirely absent) and DH (Potterwatch obsession — the visceral daily terror for his family — absent). The Sirius relationship in GoF (cave scene) is entirely absent. The reconciliation mechanisms in PoA (Hagrid-mediated hug rather than organic) and GoF (Ron retroactively claiming credit) slightly alter the emotional honesty of those relationship dynamics.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Per-book scores were uniformly 7 across all seven books — a remarkably consistent finding reflecting the same pattern repeated: Harry-Ron core intact, Hermione-Ron emotional texture compressed toward jealousy/banter at the expense of warmth, family dynamics significantly thinned, and specific secondary relationships (Sirius in GoF, Percy in OotP) entirely absent. The synthesis score of 7 directly reflects this consistent finding — relationships are functionally present and emotionally recognizable in their core dynamics, but consistently missing the sustained texture and secondary dimensions that give them their book richness.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Ron's complexity across the series derives from the coexistence of contradictory traits that are never fully resolved: simultaneously loyal and capable of petty cruelty; brave and anxious; funny and morally perceptive; warm and sometimes unkind; smart in practical ways and dismissive of intellectual effort. His class anxiety (poverty, secondhand things, being the sixth Weasley) gives his reactions consistent subtext. His capacity for emotional intelligence — comforting Hermione in DH, the tea-for-Hagrid instinct in PoA, his tact about Mad-Eye's death — surprises even attentive readers because it coexists with frequent clumsiness. His intellectual contributions (Unbreakable Vow deduction in HBP, Riddle award connection in CoS, Chamber entry in DH, ghoul plan in DH) reveal a practical intelligence that the books never fully acknowledge as intelligence, making it more authentic. The sustained unpleasantness — weeks of coldness to Hermione in HBP and GoF, the extended departure in DH, the aggression of the GoF estrangement — is where his complexity is most visible.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve Ron's broad contradictions: he is brave and insecure, funny and occasionally cruel, loyal and jealous. Individual nuanced moments survive: the Deluminator speech in DH, the 'I let you sleep in my bed' disgust in PoA, the dormitory skin conversation in HBP, the love-potion sequence. Rupert Grint's performance consistently conveys more nuance than the scripts give him — his physical comedy, his timing, and his warmth add texture that the written dialogue alone would not generate.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films systematically lose the accumulated small-moment texture that makes book-Ron complex rather than merely likeable. The socioeconomic subtext (secondhand things, family poverty anxiety) is present in at most one scene per film and absent from most. The sustained unpleasantness — the defining feature of Ron in HBP's middle section and GoF's estrangement — is consistently compressed to single scenes, removing the behavioral patterns that demonstrate genuine character complexity. Ron's nurturing emotional intelligence is almost entirely absent from the films. His intellectual contributions that are most revealing of his character (the ghoul plan as love, the Potterwatch obsession as daily terror, the Buckbeak research as moral reparation) are largely absent. OotP's entire complexity architecture — the Quidditch Keeper arc, the prefect badge, Percy's letter, the dormitory conversations — is absent. The result is a film Ron who is consistently more likeable and less uncomfortable than the book Ron, which is precisely the wrong direction for a character whose complexity depends on being sometimes genuinely difficult.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Per-book scores ranged from 8 (OotP) to 10 (PoA), with most at 9. OotP's 8 is the worst individual failure — virtually all nuance absent. PoA's 10 is the best — the most density of preserved complexity. The synthesis score of 9 reflects: broad contradictions preserved and Grint's performance adding texture; systematic loss of socioeconomic subtext, nurturing intelligence, sustained unpleasantness, and small-moment accumulative texture across all seven films; OotP and HBP as the worst failures weighted appropriately. The 9 sits in the 'noticeable simplification; important nuances, relationships, agency, or contradictions are missing' band — the character is recognizable but substantially flatter than the source.

comparative.key_observations: The synthesis score of 67 reflects a consistent and coherent pattern across all seven books: the films preserve Ron Weasley's emotional core with genuine fidelity but systematically simplify the character in every dimension that requires sustained behavioral development rather than single-scene dramatic payoff. Rupert Grint's performance is frequently better than what the scripts give him, and the warmth, loyalty, humor, and bravery that define Ron most visibly are well-served by the adaptations. The chess sacrifice, the Shrieking Shack protection, the Horcrux destructions, the departure-and-return in DH, the Chamber of Secrets initiative — the films' Ron has real dramatic moments that honor the character. The failure is systematic rather than random: every dimension shows the same compression pattern. The most important books for Ron's series-level arc — GoF (estrangement and jealousy), OotP (insecurity and triumph), HBP (romantic arc maturation), and DH (co-protagonist coming of age) — all show meaningful simplification in multiple dimensions. The single worst individual book adaptation for Ron is OotP, where virtually his entire arc (Quidditch Keeper triumph, prefect recognition, Percy's letter) is absent from the theatrical film, leaving him as a functional but almost characterless supporting presence. The second worst is HBP, where the weeks of sustained emotional dysfunction that are Ron's defining characterization in that book are compressed to episodic comedy beats. The core finding is directional rather than distortive: the films never portray Ron as something he is not, but they consistently prioritize his warmth and humor at the expense of his capacity for petty cruelty, prolonged dysfunction, and the specific social anxiety of perpetual secondness. The result is a Ron who is pleasant to watch across eight films but who lacks the full complexity, contradiction, and hard-earned growth of his book counterpart — a character rendered in two dimensions when the source material offers three.
